newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Sydney hoteliers take comfort from bed-tax deal.
newsitem.headline: Sydney hoteliers take comfort from bed-tax deal.

text.p: Hoteliers in the Olympic city of Sydney looked likely to sleep easier on Tuesday after winning a partial reprieve from the New South Wales state government on its planned bed tax.

The accomodation levy, announced in the state budget and applying only to hotels the central business district in Sydney, will now be phased in at a reduced rate over a 12-month period after a compromise was thrashed out between the hotel industry and the state government.
"The outcome was as good as I think we all could have hoped for," David Charles, chief executive of the Australian hotels Association (AHA) told reporters.
The AHA said the new agreement would cost hotels A$40 million less than the original proposal.
When announced in May, the tax was decried by industry members as certain to cost jobs and generate lower tourism earnings for the state.
Travel agents in Japan -- Australia's most lucrative tourist market -- warned that the tax could cut tourist arrivals.
Under the compromise, the tax will now be reduced from the original 10 percent to five percent at the start of the phasing-in period in September.

It will rise from five percent to seven percent on April 1, 1998 and to 10 percent on September 1, 1998. However, the compromise only applies to hotels that enter agreements to provide rooms for the Sydney 2000 Olympic Games organising body, SOCOG.
Hotels that do not sign agreements with SOCOG by December 31 this year will pay the full 10 percent from September 1, 1997.

The AHA's Charles said the compromise cleared the way for hotels to sign the SOCOG agreements, many of which were put on hold when the government sprung the surprise tax in its 1997/98 budget, provoking the government to threaten it could legislate to make rooms available for SOCOG's 2000 commitments.
"People will be negotiating in a furious manner over the next few months and we intend to finalise them by the end of this year," Charles said.

Other changes negotiated to the government's original proposal include quarterly rather than monthly tax payments, and the exemption of pre-contracted bookings -- some A$140 million of inbound traffic was affected according to the AHA.
The tax now applies to the net room rate after agent's commissions and the like.
Hotel operators listed on the Australian Stock Exchange were mixed by 2.40 p.m. (0440 GMT) with the broader market weakness restraining any moves in the thinly traded stocks.
Amalgamated Holdings was down two at A$7.26, Tourism Asset Holdings was steady at A$1.32, AAPC Ltd was down two at 83 cents as was Thakral Holdings at 85 cents.
